title: Inference chunking, latency throttling & timeout replay demo
summary: Redwood AE+SE walked through an edge-case demo focused on how the Redwood runtime handles very long contexts with chunked requests, high request-per-second bursts with throttling, and a timeout/replay workflow for partially-completed responses. Customer emphasized e2e latency SLOs for clinical summarization and strict audit trails. SE ran a short live replay of a timeout condition and showed console traces and Optimize suggestions. Next steps: share timeout replay logs, run a 24-hour POC with sample dataset, and follow up on dedicated capacity quotes and SOC2 docs.
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-01-11
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration approx: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Aisha (CTO, Polaris), Ravi (ML Eng), Jordan (Infra), Sam (PM)

[00:00:02] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, can you hear me okay?
[00:00:08] Aisha: yep loud and clear, thanks for doing this on short notice — we wanted to see failure modes we saw in staging.
[00:00:16] Liam: cool, we'll try to reproduce two things you flagged: the long note summaries where context goes to ~200k tokens and the bursty API traffic that caused a few 504s, also we'll demo the timeout-replay path.
[00:00:30] Ravi: quick context — our workflow sends consecutive patient notes as one rolling conversation. sometimes we chunk them on client side but processes patch them together. we saw slowdowns when sequence length exceeded 64k tokens.
[00:00:44] Jordan: and infra saw spikes around mid-day where TPS went from 50 to 1200 for a minute during batch jobs. we had some upstream back-off and then request timeouts.
[00:00:56] Liam: got it. first quick architecture reminder — Redwood's runtime prefers continuous KV caching and server-side chunking for huge context. if you pre-chunk incorrectly it can blow up token counts and prevent cache hits.
[00:01:10] Maya: we'll show the Console traces, an Optimize suggestion card for chunking thresholds, and then run a short live replay of a timeout and how the client can replay with idempotent session keys.

--- Quick Demo: Console & Optimize ---
[00:01:40] Liam: opening the Console now — here's a trace for the failed job you uploaded (reference: polaris-jan9-failure-1). you can see request spikes, per-token latency, and a sudden queue length bump.
[00:01:58] [00:02:00] Liam: note the green bars — those are successful streaming bytes; the orange is where the proxy throttled to keep latency SLO. there is a blue stripe at the end where the client dropped the connection, so server kept the partial KV cache but client didn't resume.
[00:02:19] Sam: what does that mean for our replay logic? can we replay a partial session and get consistent output?
[00:02:25] Liam: yes, if you use session IDs and the Redis-backed prefix store we expose. default behavior: we keep a short-lived prefix cache for 5 minutes, you can extend that. we also have a replay API: send the last acked token index and the server will continue. it's not magic — if the model is nondeterministic you'll see some variation, but it's usually stable for summarize tasks.
[00:02:48] Jordan: you said default 5 minutes — we need auditability; how does that interact with retention and KMS?
[00:02:54] Liam: retention is configurable per model route. for Private deployments you can hook into your KMS/HSM. Console shows an audit log entry for each resume/replay. note: our hosted plan keeps ephemeral KV on the node; Dedicated lets you pin cache persistence across restarts.

--- Reproducing long-context chunking ---
[00:03:20] Liam: i'm going to run the chunked ingestion test — first run client-side chunking at 128KB windows, then server-side continuous streaming with our chunk reassembler.
[00:03:36] [00:03:40] Liam: (typing) launching job demo-longcontext-128k... sending 250 messages to create a ~140k token session.
[00:04:05] Aisha: while that runs, we had two workarounds in staging: prebaked summarization and dropping older notes. both impacted clinical fidelity, so not ideal.
[00:04:16] Liam: you'll see in the trace that when you split on sentence boundaries you get much better prefix hits versus naive fixed-size chunking. Optimize suggests a dynamic chunk size keyed by average sentence length — that's the recommendation card you saw.
[00:04:40] [00:04:42] Ravi: are these suggestions model-specific? we run two model families — a 30B quantized and a 7B low-latency.
[00:04:48] Liam: yes, Optimize profiles per model. for the 30B we recommend larger chunk windows to amortize KV overhead; for 7B you can pick smaller windows and more aggressive caching. there's a per-route tuning drop-down in Console.

--- Bursty TPS & throttling ---
[00:05:20] Liam: next i'll simulate a TPS spike using the avr-burst tool — this mimics your mid-day spike.
[00:05:28] [00:05:30] Liam: (runs) sending 1400 RPS for 45s against the hosted route.
[00:05:45] [00:05:48] Maya: watchers: you'll see graceful degradations: our router sheds to cheaper model variants under pressure and enforces per-client rate limits to protect shared pools.
[00:06:02] Jordan: in our run we observed 504s coming back from your endpoint, which we assumed was an egress time out — is that from your side or from our proxy?
[00:06:09] Liam: the 504s are usually from either client or an upstream LB hit. Console's trace shows these were server-side queue timeouts: queue grew above the configured threshold so the router dropped older requests. we can tune that threshold or grant you Dedicated capacity to avoid shedding.
[00:06:25] Ravi: we may not be able to get Dedicated immediately. can we change client behavior so the UX doesn't surface errors?
[00:06:31] Liam: yes — best practice is exponential backoff with jitter and an idempotent session key so retries don't double-charge tokens. also our SDK supports automatic throttling hints returned in response headers (x-rw-throttle-hint) so clients can slow down before outright timeouts.

--- Timeout & Replay walkthrough ---
[00:07:00] Liam: now for the timeout replay. i'm going to force-close the client after partial stream and then replay from the last acked index.
[00:07:10] [00:07:12] Liam: (runs) initiating partial stream, closing after 12 seconds...
[00:07:25] Aisha: that's exactly what we saw — app closed due to perceived UX lag and users retried which created more load.
[00:07:31] Liam: exactly — there's a pattern: user retries amplify load and cause a thundering herd. our recommended approach is client-side optimistic render (render partials) and then background replay. when you replay, send the session-id + last-token-index; the runtime will attempt continuation and you'll get a status code 200 with a header x-rw-resume=true if resumed.
[00:07:52] Sam: are there any caveats when resuming with quantized models? we saw truncation artifacts in 7b-quant.
[00:07:58] Liam: quantized models sometimes introduce slight distribution shift, but truncation usually comes from tokenization boundaries. ensure you resume on token boundaries — our SDK exposes token-index markers. Also check the compiled kernel path in Console; sometimes resumes pick a different kernel if load shifts, that's visible in the trace.

--- Observability & Logs ---
[00:08:30] Liam: diving into logs: here's an example where a high-latency kernel selection increased per-token latency by 15ms which, over 20k tokens, adds minutes. Console flags these as 'kernel hot swap' events.
[00:08:45] Jordan: can we hotfix kernel selection heuristics? in Private, we'd expect more control.
[00:08:49] Liam: in Dedicated/Private yes, you can lock kernel families or pin quantization. hosted is adaptive by default but we surface the choice and suggest pinning when you want consistency.

--- Client-side mitigation patterns ---
[00:09:10] Maya: quick checklist of client patterns we recommend: idempotent session IDs, exponential backoff with jitter, optimistic partial rendering, server-side chunk reassembly enabled, and using Optimize-suggested chunk windows.
[00:09:24] Ravi: about optimistic rendering — if we render partials we risk exposing incomplete clinical notes. any guard rails?
[00:09:30] Liam: yes, tag partials as provisional and don't commit to DB until full confirmation arrives. also you can enable redact-on-fail in the backend — if replay fails, partials are marked and audit log notes the event.

--- Q&A and edge cases ---
[00:09:52] Aisha: security: we need SOC2 type II, SAML SSO, full audit logs, and KMS. what's the path for hosting in our VPC?
[00:10:02] Maya: for SOC2 and SSO we have a compliance pack (link shared) and a Private deployment option that sits in your VPC. KMS/HSM is supported in Private; for Dedicated we can enable envelope encryption and customer-managed keys. we'll send SOC2 artifacts and a Private deployment runbook after this call.
[00:10:20] Jordan: latency SLO — we need p95 under 350ms for 4k token inferences. can you meet that baseline at scale?
[00:10:28] Liam: p95 for 4k depends on model size and instance type. with our Dedicated inferents optimized for the 7B family we've seen p95 ~180-230ms on proper hardware. for 30B expect 600–800ms unless you pin quantizations and kernel optimizations. we can run a benchmark with your payload to give realistic numbers.

--- Live failure replay (short) ---
[00:11:00] Liam: launching timeout-replay-demo-run... forcing a mid-stream close, then pausing and resuming with session id polaris-session-44.
[00:11:12] [00:11:20] Liam: (typing) replay request sent with lastAck=1224...
[00:11:32] Liam: server responded 200, x-rw-resume=true, continuation appended. console shows partial response was in node 7, resume executed on node 12 due to ephemeral scheduling — see variance in kernel path.
[00:11:48] Ravi: that's likely why we saw slightly different wording in resumed outputs earlier.
[00:11:52] Liam: yep — two things to mitigate: pin node affinity for sessions longer than X minutes (configurable) or increase prefix persistence so resume keeps same node affinity.

--- Discussing tradeoffs ---
[00:12:20] Maya: tradeoff recap: you can get best consistency by pinning affinity and persistence (cost up), or get lower cost by letting the router be adaptive (slightly variable outputs). it depends on your correctness SLO for clinical notes.
[00:12:34] Aisha: our clinical compliance team will push for determinism and full audit. likely we'd prefer Dedicated or Private.
[00:12:40] Maya: totally understood. we can scope a Dedicated POC with those constraints.

--- Action Items & Next Steps ---
[00:13:00] Maya: quick recap of what we'll do next and who owns it:
[00:13:05] Maya: we'll share the timeout replay logs and the console trace exports now, and follow up with a dedicated benchmark plan for your payload.
[00:13:14] Ravi: we'll share a representative dataset (anonymized) and traffic pattern for a 24-hour POC.
[00:13:18] Jordan: and we need SOC2 paperwork and the Private deployment runbook.
[00:13:22] Maya: yes — we'll send SOC2 pack, runbook, and a Dedicated quote. also we'll provision a sandbox route for the 24-hour POC.
[00:13:30] Aisha: timeline: can we get a sandbox by next Tuesday?
[00:13:33] Maya: yes we can aim for that.

--- Closing ---
[00:13:42] Maya: thanks all — we'll email the artifacts and schedule the benchmark kickoff. any last questions?
[00:13:50] Sam: none from me, thanks.
[00:13:52] Aisha: thanks, that demo was super helpful.
[00:13:56] Liam: thanks everyone, will follow up with logs and the replay artifacts.

Note: transcription includes some mis-heard acronyms (K-V cash, V-P-C) and intermittent punctuation errors typical of automated transcripts.
